Signal to Interference plus Noise Ratio (SINR)
RSSI measures everything, RSRP measures only the useful signal.
RSSI (Received Signal Strength Indicator) measures the total power received by your phone, including useful signal, interference, and background noise. It is a broader measurement than RSRP.
If RSSI is much higher than RSRP, there is significant interference in your environment.
If RSSI is close to RSRP, the signal is clean with minimal interference.
Wi-Fi networks: RSSI is the primary signal metric
2G/GSM networks: RSSI is more commonly used
Signal proximity check: good for quick checks
Signal level is within normal range.
Signal is present but may have interference.
Signal is low. Check if you are in an area with good coverage.
n78/n79 are the most mainstream high-speed 5G bands — extremely fast but with weaker penetration, best used outdoors.
n41 is the mainstream 5G band, balancing coverage and speed — the core of China\'s 5G network.
B1/B3/B39/B40/B41 are mainstream 4G bands, offering broad coverage and balanced speeds — the backbone of mobile networks.
%s is a low-frequency band with wide coverage and strong wall penetration, but relatively slower speeds — ideal for indoor and long-distance use.

A frequency band is a specific range of radio frequencies allocated for wireless communication, like different lanes on a highway. Each band has unique characteristics: higher frequencies offer faster speeds but shorter range and weaker penetration.
Wide coverage, strong penetration. Ideal for rural areas and wide-area deployment.
Balanced coverage and speed. The primary band for urban and suburban areas.
Extremely fast but limited coverage. Best for hotspots and dense urban areas.
%s is a high-speed band. Your 5G experience should be excellent!
%s is a mid-band, balancing speed and coverage. For faster speeds, try moving closer to a 5G tower.
%s is a low band with stable coverage but slower speeds. Best for indoor and long-distance use.

If PCI changes frequently, you are at the boundary between two cell towers.

PCI (Physical Cell ID) is a unique identifier assigned to each cell sector by the network. It helps your phone distinguish between neighboring cell towers. PCI values range from 0 to 1007 (4G LTE) or 0 to 1007 (5G NR).
Normal handover: PCI changes when you move between cells
When you move from one cell tower coverage area to another, your phone automatically switches to the stronger signal, and the PCI changes accordingly.
If PCI changes rapidly (several times per minute), you are likely at a cell tower boundary or experiencing signal instability.
In 4G LTE networks, PCI Mod 3 should not be the same for neighboring cells, otherwise signal interference occurs. This is why PCI planning is important for network operators.
Current PCI is stable. Your connection is maintaining a consistent cell tower.
PCI has changed. Your phone has handed over to a new cell tower.
EARFCN can be used to calculate the exact frequency in MHz.

EARFCN (E-UTRA Absolute Radio Frequency Channel Number) is a number that represents the exact center frequency of a cell. Network operators use it to identify the specific channel a cell tower is broadcasting on.
Each EARFCN corresponds to a specific downlink frequency in MHz.
China Mobile: B3 (1800MHz), B8 (900MHz), B39 (1900MHz), n41 (2.6GHz), n79 (4.9GHz)
China Unicom: B1 (2100MHz), B3 (1800MHz), B8 (900MHz), n1 (2.1GHz), n78 (3.5GHz)
China Telecom: B1 (2100MHz), B3 (1800MHz), B5 (850MHz), n78 (3.5GHz)
Your phone is connected to a specific frequency channel. Different channels within the same band have similar performance characteristics.
TAC changes less frequently than PCI, usually when you travel to a new area.

TAC (Tracking Area Code) is a number assigned to a group of cell towers in a specific geographic area. Network operators use TAC to manage paging — when someone calls you, the network only pages the cell towers within your current TAC, not the entire network.
Moving to a new district or city center
Subway or train passing through different zones
Flying into a new city (airport arrival)
Efficient paging: Only pages the cell towers in your current area
Location tracking: Helps the network know which region you are in
Load balancing: Prevents the network from wasting resources
Current TAC is stable. Your location area has not changed.
TAC has changed. You have entered a new tracking area.
PCI is available on all networks (2G/3G/4G/5G), named differently per protocol (PCI/PSC/CID)
EARFCN is available on 4G LTE, 5G NR, and 3G WCDMA. 2G GSM does not support this parameter
TAC is used on 4G LTE and 5G NR. 3G WCDMA and 2G GSM use LAC (Location Area Code) instead
RSRP/SS-RSRP is available on 4G LTE and 5G NR. 3G WCDMA and 2G GSM do not support it
RSRQ/SS-RSRQ is available on 4G LTE and 5G NR. 3G WCDMA and 2G GSM do not support it
SINR is available on 4G LTE (via RSSNR) and 5G NR. 3G WCDMA and 2G GSM do not support it

RSSI is available via API on 2G GSM and 4G LTE. 5G NR has RSSI in its protocol (used to compute SS-RSRQ), but Google chose not to expose it to apps due to TDD/beamforming causing unreliable wide fluctuations
Band info is available on 4G LTE and 5G NR. 3G WCDMA and 2G GSM do not support it

Controls how often the app polls signal data. Fast (2s) for intensive monitoring, Slow (5s) for battery saving. Actual interval is subject to system scheduling — some devices may not reach 2s
RSRQ must be read together with RSRP to judge signal conditions reliably.
RSRP (Reference Signal Received Power) is the power of the reference signal your phone measures from the tower. It is the core metric for 4G/5G coverage strength.
Very strong signal, peak throughput, HD VoLTE, seamless handover
Good signal, stable high-speed data, smooth everyday use
Moderate signal, throughput starts to drop, indoor attenuation possible
Weak signal, noticeably lower throughput, higher latency, possible drops
Extremely weak signal, only a minimal connection, possibly no service
Distance to the tower: the farther away, the weaker the signal
Building obstruction: reinforced concrete walls attenuate heavily
Weather: heavy rain or fog causes slight attenuation
User density: signal fluctuates when the tower is heavily loaded
Excellent signal! You are close to the tower — 5G can reach peak rates with the lowest latency.
Good signal, smooth for everyday use. If it feels slow, try adjusting your position.
Moderate signal, speed may drop. Move near a window or outdoors.
Weak signal. Move near a window or outdoors and avoid obstructions.
Extremely weak signal — you may be at the cell edge or in a dead zone.
RSRQ (Reference Signal Received Quality) measures how clean the signal is. Even with strong RSRP, heavy interference will drag down real-world speed.
Clean signal, low cell load, excellent experience
Some interference or higher load, still usable overall
Heavy interference or an overloaded cell, unstable speed — common in crowded places
Strong RSRP + Good RSRQ = excellent quality!
Both strength and purity are good — the ideal network state.
Strong RSRP + Poor RSRQ = high interference
Strength is sufficient but interference is high. Common in crowded stations and malls.
Weak RSRP + Poor RSRQ = poor signal
Both strength and purity are poor. Move outdoors or near a window.
High signal purity with little interference — a very good experience.
Some interference, but if RSRP is strong the experience is still acceptable.
Heavy interference. Move away from crowded areas or large electronic equipment.
SINR is the key metric for real-world speed — more informative than RSRP.
SINR (Signal to Interference plus Noise Ratio) compares useful signal against interference and noise. Imagine hearing someone in a noisy room — the voice is the signal, the crowd is the noise.
5G: 5-30 Mbps / 4G: < 10 Mbps, low-speed QPSK, high latency
Signal is buried in noise, frequent retransmissions, connection may not hold
Closer to the tower means a stronger signal and higher SINR
Crowds increase interference and lower SINR
Frequent handovers at cell edges can make SINR fluctuate
Excellent SINR! 5G can reach 500 Mbps+, 4G 80 Mbps+, with the most efficient modulation.
Good SINR — 5G can reach 300-500 Mbps, comfortable for everyday use.
Moderate SINR — 5G around 30-250 Mbps. Video streams fine but large downloads are slow.
Poor SINR — 5G below 30 Mbps. Move to an open area to improve the environment.
Very poor SINR — the signal is almost buried in noise. Move to a location with better coverage.
Monitor 2G/3G/4G/5G cellular signals in real time and understand your network environment.

Signal Insight does not request the network permission at all. Check this app\'s permission list in system settings — there is no network entry. All data is processed locally and can never be uploaded or leaked to any server.
Reads cell signal strength, SIM status and network type — the core functionality this app depends on.
Android requires location permission to read cell information. This app never records or tracks your actual location.
This project is open source under the Apache 2.0 license, with source code hosted on GitHub.

Note: 3GPP only specifies RSRP reporting range and accuracy, not what counts as good. The table above is a common industry rule of thumb; vendors and operators differ slightly. This app uses the same thresholds for assessment and scoring.

Note: RSRQ\'s theoretical ceiling is about -3 dB (single antenna port, unloaded, no interference) and is rarely reached in practice. A typical single-port fully loaded cell reads about -10.8 dB; two-port cells read about -6 dB unloaded and -13 dB loaded. Cell load alone can shift RSRQ by 7-8 dB, so variation at the same location over time is normal. 3GPP only defines its reporting range (about -19.5 to -3 dB, 0.5 dB steps), not its grading.

Note: Real throughput does not depend on SINR alone. 3GPP does not define a SINR-to-throughput conversion; each chipset vendor builds its own mapping from measurement. Actual speed also depends on bandwidth, MIMO layers, scheduling, network congestion and device capability, and modulation order does not map one-to-one to SINR. The table above is indicative only.
An important property: RSSI rises with cell load
Even when the radio link itself is unchanged, RSSI increases as more users in the cell raise total transmit power. A higher RSSI therefore does not necessarily mean a better signal.

Note: TAC itself does not perform load balancing. Load balancing is handled by cell selection, reselection and handover policies. Tracking Area List planning does consider paging signalling volume, but that is a network-planning concern rather than a function of TAC.

Note: 700 MHz (n28) is led by China Broadcasting Network, with China Mobile sharing it under network co-construction. An n28 cell may therefore also appear on China Mobile. Operator band usage changes with co-construction and network tuning; only major bands are listed here.

Fdl_low is the band\'s downlink start frequency, Ndl the corresponding start channel number, with 0.1 MHz steps. For band B3, Fdl_low = 1805 MHz and Ndl = 1200, so EARFCN 1500 maps to 1805 + 0.1 x (1500 - 1200) = 1835 MHz.
